 John Madden, the Raiders coach whose name outgrew his own record
 Photo: Unknown author / Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons — Wikimedia Commons 
 By 
 Penelope H. Fritz 
 5 min read 
 Add us on Google 
 John Madden Photo: Unknown authorUnknown author / Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Born April 10, 1936
 Austin 
 Died December 28, 2021 (85) 
 Occupation Footballer 
 Honours Super Bowl 
 Individual awards Sports Lifetime Achievement Award · California Hall of Fame · Pro Football Hall of Fame 
 Ask a twenty-year-old who John Madden was and the answer will probably be a video game. Their parents will picture a big man drawing yellow circles over a replay and shouting “Boom!” into a headset. Only people old enough to have watched the Oakland Raiders in the years of the Immaculate Reception start with the coaching record, which is the part that put him in the Hall of Fame and the part the other two versions buried. Now there is a fourth Madden: Nicolas Cage under prosthetics in David O. Russell’s Madden on Prime Video .
 He was a mechanic’s son. Earl Madden moved the family from southern Minnesota to Daly City, just south of San Francisco, when John was small, and the boy grew into an offensive tackle good enough to earn a scholarship. A knee injury at Oregon sent him back through two junior colleges before he settled at Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo, where he played on both sides of the ball and studied education. The Philadelphia Eagles drafted him in a late round, and in his first training camp he tore a knee ligament. He never played a regular-season game in the NFL.
 John Earl Madden was born on April 10, 1936, in Austin, Minnesota, and the injury that ended his playing career in 1959 is the reason he became a coach. Rehabbing in Philadelphia, he sat in on film sessions with the quarterback Norm Van Brocklin. “I ended up with a degree in teaching and my love for football meshed with teaching,” he said later. In October 1960 a plane carrying the Cal Poly football team crashed, killing 16 players and others close to him. He coached at Allan Hancock College in Santa Maria, then spent three seasons as a defensive assistant at San Diego State under Don Coryell, whom he credited as an influence.
 Al Davis hired him as linebackers coach of the Raiders in 1967 and, on February 4, 1969, made him head coach. Madden was 32, the youngest head coach in professional football at the time. Over the next ten seasons his teams went 103-32-7 in the regular season and never had a losing year. He reached 100 regular-season victories younger than any coach before him. No coach who has led a team for at least 100 NFL games has a better winning percentage, and no Raiders coach has won more.
 The record hides how often those teams lost the game that mattered. Madden’s Raiders reached seven AFL or AFC championship games and lost six of them. In December 1972 a deflected pass that Franco Harris scooped up, the Immaculate Reception, turned a Raiders playoff win into a 13-7 loss in Pittsburgh. The Steelers beat them again in the AFC title games after the 1974 and 1975 seasons. In 1976 Oakland finally went through Pittsburgh, 24-7, and on January 9, 1977, beat the Minnesota Vikings 32-14 in Super Bowl XI. Two seasons later, at 42, with an ulcer and what he called burnout, he quit. He said it was permanent, and it was.
 Television made him bigger than coaching ever had. CBS hired him in 1979, and from 1981 he formed the network’s lead NFL team with Pat Summerall; the two called eight Super Bowls together. When Fox took the NFC package from CBS in 1994, the pair moved with it, lending the new network credibility, and Fox paid Madden more each year than any NFL player earned. He moved to ABC’s Monday Night Football with Al Michaels in 2002 and to NBC’s Sunday night games in 2006, the first broadcaster to work for all four major American networks. He won 16 Sports Emmy Awards and made the telestrator a fixture of sports television. He called his last game, Super Bowl XLIII, in February 2009 and retired that April.
 He did all of it without flying. After a panic attack on a flight out of Tampa in 1979 he never boarded a plane again; he crossed the country on Amtrak and, from 1987, in the Madden Cruiser, a custom bus supplied by Greyhound. In 1984 the Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins approached him about a football game for home computers. The early design put fewer than eleven players on each side, and Madden refused to put his name on anything that was not real football. John Madden Football arrived in 1988 with eleven a side, and the series that became Madden NFL grew into the best-selling American football video game franchise. He treated it as a teaching tool, “a way for people to learn the game and participate in the game at a pretty sophisticated level,” as he put it in 2012.
 The success cost his sideline reputation. Many fans came to know him first as a cover image, and the Miller Lite commercials of the 1980s had already sold him as a lovable, bumbling big man, a caricature of a coach whose degree was in teaching. The Pro Football Hall of Fame took its time as well. Madden had been eligible for 27 years when the Seniors Committee put him forward, and when he was inducted in August 2006 the Hall made a point of saying he went in on his coaching merits. That it needed saying is the story.
 Away from the cameras his life stayed in Pleasanton, east of Oakland. He married Virginia Fields, whom he met as a student in a bar in Pismo Beach, on December 26, 1959. They had two sons, Joseph and Michael, and a grandson, Jesse, joined the Washington Commanders as an assistant coach in 2025. Fox aired the documentary All Madden on Christmas Day 2021. Three days later, on December 28, Madden died at home, aged 85, two days after his 62nd wedding anniversary.
 The name has kept working since. The NFL turned its Thanksgiving tripleheader into the John Madden Thanksgiving Celebration in 2022, and every edition of Madden NFL 23 carried his picture on the cover. In June 2026 Cal Poly opened the $45 million John Madden Football Center, built beside the memorial to the victims of the 1960 crash, and later retired his No. 74. On November 18, 2026, Prime Video released Madden , written and directed by Russell, with Cage as Madden, Christian Bale as Al Davis and Kathryn Hahn as Virginia, after a brief run in select US theaters rather than a wide release.
 Cage’s version is the fourth John Madden, after the coach, the voice and the game, and it will not be the last. EA puts out a new edition every year, in front of players who never saw him coach a down. Each one still carries the condition he set before he signed anything: eleven players a side, or not his name.
